scope: General educational automotive guidance. This collection does not replace vehicle-specific service information, inspection, or professional diagnosis.

documents.title: Engine misfire, rough idle, stalling, or loss of power
keywords: what does a spark plug do
what does an ignition coil do
documents.overview: A misfire or rough-running complaint means the engine is not producing smooth, consistent power. The symptom alone does not identify a failed part.
component_functions: Spark plugs provide the ignition spark in spark-ignition engines; ignition coils supply the required high voltage.
Fuel injectors meter fuel into the engine according to the engine-control system.
A fuel pump supplies fuel at the system's required pressure; its design differs by vehicle.
possible_causes: Ignition, fuel delivery, air intake, sensor, compression, or wiring problems can produce similar symptoms.
symptoms: Uneven idle, hesitation, shaking, reduced power, stalling, or a flashing malfunction indicator may occur.
checks: Note when the symptom occurs and whether a warning light is steady or flashing.
Have diagnostic trouble codes and related data read before parts are replaced.
documents.urgency: A flashing engine warning light, severe shaking, fuel smell, or stalling can indicate a condition that may damage the vehicle or create a hazard. Stop safely and arrange qualified assistance.
needed_information: Make, model, year, engine, mileage, warning lights, diagnostic codes, and when the symptom occurs.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Use the manual for the exact vehicle and engine; do not assume one diagnostic procedure applies to all vehicles.

documents.title: Engine overheating and cooling-system concerns
keywords: what causes an engine to overheat
documents.overview: An overheating indication means heat is not being removed or circulated as intended, or the temperature reading is not trustworthy. Treat a high-temperature warning as real until the vehicle-specific checks establish otherwise. The cooling system moves heat from the engine through coolant and heat exchangers; radiator airflow, coolant circulation, system sealing, and temperature control all matter.
component_functions: Coolant absorbs engine heat and carries it to a radiator or other heat exchanger.
The radiator transfers heat from coolant to airflow; blocked external fins or restricted internal flow can reduce heat rejection.

A thermostat controls coolant flow according to engine design. A thermostat stuck closed or opening late can restrict heat transfer; a thermostat stuck open more commonly causes slow warm-up rather than classic overheating.
A coolant pump circulates coolant. A damaged impeller, drive problem, or leak can reduce circulation; pump design and drive method vary by vehicle.
Cooling fans increase airflow at low road speed or when commanded. Fan operation is controlled differently across vehicles and may not be obvious from a brief visual check.
The pressure cap and sealed system raise the coolant boiling margin and control pressure. A weak cap, leak, or trapped air can cause coolant loss or poor circulation; never open a hot system.
possible_causes: Coolant loss from a hose, radiator, reservoir, heater circuit, pump seal, or another connection reduces the amount of heat-carrying fluid; a leak may appear only when hot or pressurized.

A radiator or heat-exchanger restriction, damaged fins, blocked grille, debris, or obstructed airflow can prevent enough heat from leaving the coolant, often becoming more apparent under load or hot weather.
A cooling fan, fan relay/control, wiring, fuse, or temperature input problem can reduce airflow at idle or in traffic; temperature that improves at road speed is a clue, not proof.
A thermostat that does not open as intended can limit circulation through the radiator. Housing or hose temperatures alone are not a definitive test.
A coolant-pump circulation or drive problem can reduce coolant flow and cause overheating at different speeds; leaks or noise may be present but are not required.
Air trapped after service, incorrect filling/bleeding, or a system leak can interrupt circulation and cause fluctuating temperature or intermittent cabin heat.
A pressure-cap or sealing fault can allow premature boiling or coolant expulsion without an obvious cold leak.

Less common but serious causes include internal leakage, combustion gases entering the cooling circuit, a restricted exhaust or other engine fault increasing heat load, or an inaccurate temperature sensor/gauge. These require evidence-based testing.
symptoms: A temperature rise mainly while idling or in slow traffic, with improvement at road speed, can point toward insufficient low-speed airflow; verify fan command and operation before replacing parts.

Overheating at highway speed or under load can occur with inadequate coolant flow, restricted heat exchange, low coolant, excess engine heat load, or other faults; it does not identify a single component.
A heater that turns cold while the engine temperature rises can accompany low coolant or interrupted circulation and is an urgent warning, but heater design and control vary.
Sweet coolant odor, visible wetness, dried residue, repeated low level, or steam can support coolant loss; absence of a puddle does not rule out a hot/pressurized or internal leak.
Temperature that fluctuates, gurgling, or recent cooling-system work can be consistent with trapped air or low coolant but needs confirmation.
Persistent bubbles, rapid pressurization from a cold start, unexplained coolant loss, or white exhaust may warrant internal-leak tests; none alone proves a head-gasket failure.
checks: Never remove a radiator cap, pressurized reservoir cap, hose, or bleed screw while hot; hot coolant and steam can cause severe burns.

After the vehicle is completely cool, look from a safe position for a low level only in the reservoir and by the procedure specified in that vehicle's owner's manual. Do not top up with an unspecified fluid or open a sealed system.
Look for obvious external leakage or damage without reaching near fans, belts, or hot parts; electric fans can start unexpectedly.

Record when the temperature rises, warning messages, coolant level only when cold, visible residue, cabin-heater behavior, recent repairs, and ambient/load conditions. Do not run an overheating engine to reproduce the symptom.
diagnostic_steps: Compare the dashboard indication with scan-tool coolant-temperature data from a cold start and during a controlled test; check plausibility against ambient conditions and independent measurements using the vehicle procedure.

Inspect coolant level and condition when cold, then inspect hoses, radiator, reservoir, pump area, heater circuit, cap, and connections for evidence of leakage; use the specified pressure-test procedure when indicated.
Check commanded and actual fan operation, fan stages, fuses, relays/control module, wiring, and relevant temperature inputs using the wiring diagram and service procedure.
Evaluate thermostat opening and coolant circulation with vehicle-appropriate temperature measurements; do not infer a failed thermostat from one hose-temperature observation.

If external causes are not found, perform the relevant internal-leak checks, such as a combustion-gas test, cylinder leak-down/compression checks, or oil/coolant inspection as justified. A positive or negative result must be interpreted using the exact engine procedure.

After repair, refill and bleed using the specified coolant and procedure, verify stable temperature and fan operation under controlled conditions, check for leaks after cool-down, and confirm the warning does not return.
vehicle_variations: Cooling layouts, pressure caps, expansion tanks, thermostat locations, pump drives, fan controls, bleed procedures, and coolant specifications differ by make, model, engine, and year.
Motorcycles and some compact vehicles may have different radiator/fan packaging; pickups and vans may have additional heat exchangers or load/towing effects.

Hybrids and electric vehicles can have separate coolant circuits for the engine, power electronics, traction battery, or cabin. Do not assume one reservoir serves every circuit; high-voltage system work is for appropriately trained technicians.
known_unknowns: Without the exact vehicle and measured conditions, a specific cause cannot be ranked. No manufacturer procedure, coolant type, pressure value, or temperature threshold was available for this response.
documents.urgency: If a high-temperature warning appears, steam or coolant is expelled, or the temperature continues to rise, stop safely and switch off the engine. Do not continue driving an overheating vehicle; severe damage can occur. Arrange qualified assistance.
needed_information: Make/model/year, engine and fuel type, exact dashboard warning or gauge reading, when it overheats (idle/traffic/speed/load), whether cabin heat changes, coolant level checked only when fully cold, visible leaks/steam/odor, recent repair or coolant work, and any scan codes or measured temperatures.
documents.source_gap: No exact vehicle identity or manufacturer service document was available for this answer; the technical explanation is general and its vehicle-specific procedures remain unverified.

documents.title: Engine oil pressure, leaks, and oil consumption
keywords: red oil pressure light came on while driving
engine is using oil but no visible leak
documents.overview: Oil level, oil pressure, and oil condition are different checks. A warning lamp may indicate a lubrication problem and should not be treated as a routine reminder without checking the manual.
possible_causes: A leak, incorrect level, consumption, sensor or wiring issue, or lubrication-system fault can cause oil-related symptoms.
symptoms: Oil warning lamp, visible oil drops, smoke, burning-oil odor, or a level that repeatedly falls.
checks: If an oil-pressure warning appears while running, stop the engine as soon as it is safe.
Check the level only using the vehicle's specified procedure and correct oil specification.
Do not diagnose pressure from the dipstick level alone.
documents.urgency: An oil-pressure warning, loud engine noise, or rapid oil loss requires stopping safely and prompt qualified inspection.
needed_information: Warning symbol or message, measured level and procedure, oil specification, leak location, mileage, and service history.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Oil specification, level-check method, and warning response are vehicle-specific.

documents.title: Engine oil change timing and service schedule
keywords: when should I change engine oil
oil-life reminder versus oil pressure warning
oil-life reminder is different from red oil pressure warning
what oil grade and service interval does my vehicle need
what oil grade and service interval does my car need
oil grade and service interval for a 2022 Toyota Corolla
what does an oil filter do
documents.overview: Engine oil change timing depends on the exact engine, oil specification, operating conditions, and manufacturer schedule or oil-life monitoring system. There is no single interval that applies to every vehicle.
component_functions: Engine oil forms a lubricating film and helps manage friction and heat within the engine.
The oil filter removes contaminants from circulating oil within its designed capacity.
possible_causes: Severe operating conditions, incorrect oil specification, missed service records, or an oil-life system may change when service is due.
symptoms: A service reminder or oil-life message should be interpreted using the owner's manual; an oil-pressure warning is a separate, more urgent condition.
checks: Check the exact make/model/year/engine maintenance schedule and service history.
Use the specified oil grade and service procedure.
Do not use a general mileage interval when the vehicle maker specifies otherwise.
documents.urgency: A routine oil-change reminder is not the same as an oil-pressure warning. If oil pressure is warned while the engine is running, stop safely and follow the manual.
needed_information: Exact vehicle and engine, mileage, oil specification, last service date/odometer, and operating conditions.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and maintenance schedule
sources.reference: The manufacturer schedule and required oil specification control; no universal interval is asserted.

documents.title: Fuel delivery, air intake, sensors, and ignition
documents.overview: Fuel, air, ignition, and engine-control systems work together. Starting or power symptoms do not by themselves prove that a fuel pump, sensor, coil, or spark plug has failed.
possible_causes: Battery condition, fuel supply, ignition components, air leaks, wiring, sensors, or mechanical condition may be involved.
symptoms: Long cranking, rough running, hesitation, stalling, reduced power, or an engine warning light.
checks: Record whether the engine cranks, warning lights, recent repairs, and conditions when the problem occurs.
Use diagnostic testing before replacing components.
documents.urgency: A fuel leak or strong fuel smell is a fire risk: stop safely, avoid ignition sources, and seek assistance. Repeated stalling in traffic also needs prompt attention.
needed_information: Make/model/year/engine, cranking behavior, warning codes, fuel or repair history, and symptom conditions.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information
sources.reference: Diagnostic specifications and test procedures vary by engine and model year.

documents.title: Timing belts, timing chains, and engine wear
documents.overview: Timing components keep engine events synchronized. Whether a vehicle uses a belt or chain, inspection and replacement requirements depend on the exact engine and manufacturer schedule.
possible_causes: Age, mileage, lubrication or tensioner problems, and component wear may affect timing-system condition.
symptoms: Unusual timing-area noise or engine-running problems may warrant inspection, but symptoms cannot establish belt or chain condition.
checks: Verify the engine-specific maintenance schedule and service history.
Have suspected timing noise or damage inspected by a qualified technician.
documents.urgency: If timing-related failure is suspected or the engine suddenly runs abnormally, stop driving and arrange professional assessment.
needed_information: Exact engine, model year, mileage, maintenance records, and any noise or warning symptoms.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and maintenance schedule
sources.reference: Do not apply a generic timing-belt interval to every engine.

documents.title: Brake pads, rotors, calipers, and wear symptoms
documents.overview: Brake pads and friction surfaces wear with use. Noise or vibration can have several causes and requires inspection; it is not a measurement of remaining pad life.
component_functions: Brake pads press against a rotor or drum to create friction and slow the wheel.
Rotors or drums provide the friction surface; calipers apply pad force in many disc-brake systems.
Brake fluid transmits hydraulic force in hydraulic brake systems.
possible_causes: Worn or contaminated friction material, rotor condition, hardware, caliper movement, or other brake faults may cause noise or vibration.
symptoms: Squealing, grinding, vibration while braking, pulling, longer stopping distance, or a changed pedal feel.
checks: Do not rely on sound alone to estimate pad thickness.
Have the full brake system inspected if noise, vibration, pulling, or reduced braking occurs.
documents.urgency: Grinding, reduced braking, a soft pedal, pulling, or a brake warning requires stopping safely and prompt inspection. Do not continue a rental or trip when braking performance is impaired.
needed_information: Vehicle, symptom, warning lights, when it occurs, recent brake work, and inspection measurements if available.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Brake inspection and wear limits are vehicle-specific.

documents.title: Brake-fluid, ABS, and brake warning lights
keywords: ABS warning light is on but brake pedal feels normal
documents.overview: Brake and ABS warnings can indicate different systems. The exact symbol and the owner's-manual instructions matter; an ABS warning does not prove that the ordinary braking system is fully functional.
possible_causes: Fluid level or leakage, sensor or wiring faults, hydraulic concerns, or ABS component issues may trigger warnings.
symptoms: Brake or ABS warning lamp, fluid loss, changed pedal feel, or reduced braking.
checks: Identify the exact warning and follow the manual's immediate instructions.
Do not open or service hydraulic components unless qualified.
Arrange professional diagnostic inspection.
documents.urgency: A red brake warning with changed pedal feel, visible fluid leak, or reduced stopping ability is safety-critical. Stop safely and seek assistance.
needed_information: Exact warning icon/message, pedal feel, visible leaks, and vehicle make/model/year.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: Warning-light meanings and required response vary by vehicle.

documents.title: Transmission slipping, delayed shifting, or overheating
keywords: how does diagnosis differ for an automatic and a CVT
low or incorrect transmission fluid cause shifting problems
what is the correct transmission fluid capacity for my vehicle
documents.overview: Slipping or delayed engagement describes a driving symptom, not a confirmed transmission failure. Different transmission designs have different fluid-check and service requirements.
component_functions: A transmission provides gear ratios to match engine output to driving conditions.
A clutch in many manual vehicles connects or disconnects engine power from the transmission.
A differential allows driven wheels to rotate at different speeds while transmitting torque.
possible_causes: Fluid condition or level, control or sensor faults, clutch wear, overheating, or internal wear may contribute.
symptoms: Engine speed rises without expected acceleration, delayed engagement, harsh shifts, warning messages, or unusual noise.
checks: Avoid towing or continued hard driving when a warning or severe symptom occurs.
Check fluid only if the manufacturer's procedure permits it; many systems require special conditions or have no dipstick.
Have codes and fluid condition assessed.
documents.urgency: Loss of drive, severe slipping, burning odor, fluid leak, or an over-temperature warning warrants stopping safely and arranging inspection.
needed_information: Transmission type, vehicle details, warning codes, symptom conditions, mileage, and service history.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Fluid type and checking procedures are transmission-specific.

documents.title: Clutch, driveshaft, differential, and acceleration vibration
keywords: why does my car shake when I accelerate
documents.overview: A vibration under acceleration can originate in tires, wheels, mounts, axles, driveshafts, engine operation, or drivetrain components. The condition and speed at which it occurs help narrow inspection.
possible_causes: Wheel or tire issues, worn joints or mounts, imbalance, clutch problems, or engine misfire can create overlapping symptoms.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration during acceleration, a change with vehicle speed, noise, or engine-speed flare.
checks: Note speed, gear, steering input, and whether vibration occurs while coasting or braking.
Do not inspect under an unsupported vehicle.
Arrange an inspection if vibration is new, worsening, or accompanied by noise.
documents.urgency: Severe vibration, loss of control, loud impact noise, or a damaged tire requires stopping safely and professional help.
needed_information: Vehicle and transmission, speed/gear, acceleration conditions, tire history, noises, and warning lights.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information
sources.reference: A road test and inspection may be needed to distinguish possible causes.

documents.title: Tire pressure, tread, rotation, and replacement
documents.overview: Tires affect grip, handling, and stopping. Use the vehicle placard and owner's manual for recommended cold pressure and rotation guidance; the maximum pressure on a tire sidewall is not the vehicle's target pressure.
possible_causes: Pressure loss, wear, alignment or suspension condition, loading, and usage can affect tire condition.
symptoms: Pressure warning, visible damage, low pressure, uneven wear, vibration, or reduced wet-road grip.
checks: Check cold pressure against the vehicle placard/manual and inspect for damage.
Use a suitable tread-depth gauge or have tires inspected.
Do not drive on a visibly damaged, bulging, or rapidly deflating tire.
documents.urgency: A bulge, exposed cords, rapid pressure loss, or tire damage can cause loss of control. Stop safely and arrange assistance.
needed_information: Vehicle, tire size, measured cold pressure, tread measurement, damage, and loading.

sources.name: NHTSA Tire Safety
sources.reference: Official tire safety information.

sources.name: Vehicle tire placard and owner's manual
sources.reference: Use the pressure and maintenance guidance for the exact vehicle.

documents.title: Steering, alignment, suspension, and wheel-bearing symptoms
documents.overview: Steering and suspension symptoms affect vehicle control. Pulling, vibration, or noise can also arise from tires, brakes, road conditions, or wheel alignment.
possible_causes: Tire pressure or wear, alignment, worn suspension joints, shocks/struts, wheel bearings, or brake drag may contribute.
symptoms: Pulling, wandering, excessive bounce, clunks, vibration, uneven tire wear, or humming that changes with speed.
checks: Check tire condition and pressure only when safe.
Have steering, suspension, wheel attachment, and alignment inspected; do not work under an unsupported vehicle.
documents.urgency: Loose steering, a damaged wheel/tire, severe pulling, or a sudden change in handling is safety-critical. Stop safely and arrange inspection.
needed_information: Vehicle, speed and road conditions, recent impacts or repairs, tire condition, noises, and warning lights.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Inspection procedures and alignment specifications are vehicle-specific.

documents.title: Battery, alternator, starter, and charging-system problems
keywords: one click and will not crank
loose ground causes intermittent electrical problems
what does a starter motor do
what does a car battery do
documents.overview: Starting and charging symptoms can involve the battery, starter, alternator, wiring, connections, or another electrical load. A symptom alone cannot identify which part has failed.
component_functions: The battery stores electrical energy for starting and vehicle loads.
The starter motor turns the engine during starting.
The alternator supplies electrical power and charges the battery while the engine runs in vehicles equipped with one.
possible_causes: Low battery charge or capacity, loose/corroded connections, charging-system faults, starter issues, or parasitic electrical draw.
symptoms: Slow crank, clicking, dimming lights, battery/charging warning, repeated jump-start need, or stalling.
checks: Record warning lights and whether the problem occurs after the vehicle sits or while running.
Have battery and charging system tested with appropriate equipment.
Avoid shorting battery terminals; follow the manual for jump-starting.
documents.urgency: A burning smell, smoke, hot wiring, or repeated stalling requires stopping safely and qualified assistance.
needed_information: Battery age, starting behavior, warning lights, recent jump starts, and test results if available.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: Jump-start locations and procedures vary by vehicle.

documents.title: Dashboard warning lights and OBD diagnostic trouble codes
keywords: P0300 code does not prove spark plugs are bad
does diagnostic code P0300 prove the spark plugs are bad
documents.overview: An OBD diagnostic trouble code identifies a detected condition or circuit that needs diagnosis; it does not automatically identify a failed part. A code reader's description is not a complete diagnosis.
possible_causes: The same code can have multiple causes, including wiring, connections, leaks, sensor readings, or a component fault.
symptoms: Warning lamp, stored or pending code, drivability change, or emissions-related notice.
checks: Record exact codes and freeze-frame data before clearing them.
Follow the vehicle-specific diagnostic procedure and verify the underlying cause before replacing parts.
Use the owner's manual for warning severity.
documents.urgency: A flashing warning, oil-pressure or temperature warning, brake/steering warning, or severe drivability problem needs immediate attention. Do not treat all dashboard lights as equal.
needed_information: Exact code including prefix, warning icon, vehicle make/model/year/engine, and symptoms.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information
sources.reference: Code definitions and diagnostic tests vary by make, model, engine, and year.

documents.title: Coolant, brake, transmission, and other fluid leaks
keywords: coolant color does not prove compatibility
documents.overview: Fluid color or location alone is not reliable proof of fluid type or source. Some vehicles use different fluids or do not have a serviceable reservoir for a particular system.
possible_causes: A seal, hose, connection, reservoir, or component may leak; fluid can travel before dripping.
symptoms: Puddle, falling fluid level, odor, warning light, overheating, or changed brake/steering/transmission behavior.
checks: Do not taste or touch unknown fluid; keep people and pets away.
Do not open a hot cooling system.
A brake-fluid leak or changed pedal feel requires stopping safely; identify the source professionally.
documents.urgency: Fuel, brake-fluid, major coolant, or oil-pressure-related leaks can be hazardous. Stop safely and seek qualified assistance rather than continuing to drive.
needed_information: Leak location, approximate amount, warning lights, fluid level only if safe to check, and recent service.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: Fluid types, reservoirs, and safe checks are vehicle-specific.

documents.title: Filters, spark plugs, and routine preventive service
keywords: clogged fuel filter causes poor performance
do all cars have the same spark plug replacement interval
what does an air filter do
documents.overview: Filters and ignition items have different service requirements. Dust, operating conditions, engine design, and the manufacturer's schedule can change inspection or replacement timing.
component_functions: The engine air filter limits intake contaminants.
The cabin air filter cleans air entering the passenger compartment where fitted.
A fuel filter removes specified contaminants from fuel where the vehicle has a serviceable filter.
possible_causes: A restricted or damaged filter or worn ignition component may affect operation, but symptoms are not enough to confirm the part is due.
symptoms: Reduced airflow, odor, rough running, or a service reminder may prompt inspection but do not determine a universal interval.
checks: Use the schedule for the exact make/model/year/engine and severe-use conditions.
Record completed service and parts used.
Do not set a generic interval as overdue without the applicable schedule and service history.
documents.urgency: Routine service is generally planned maintenance; address warning lights, misfires, or unsafe symptoms promptly.
needed_information: Vehicle identity, engine, mileage, operating conditions, and dated service records.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific maintenance schedule
sources.reference: Use the manufacturer's schedule; no universal interval is asserted here.

documents.title: Mileage-based and time-based maintenance schedules
keywords: what maintenance is overdue at 60000 kilometers
calculate next service date without maintenance history
documents.overview: Maintenance may be scheduled by time, mileage, operating conditions, or a vehicle's monitoring system. Without the applicable maker schedule and verified service records, overdue status cannot be calculated reliably.
possible_causes: Missing history, incorrect mileage, severe operating conditions, or use of the wrong vehicle schedule can make a due-date estimate unreliable.
symptoms: A service reminder or missing record is a reason to check documentation, not proof that a particular component has failed.
checks: Compare dated service records and odometer readings with the exact vehicle's official schedule.
Use manufacturer severe-use guidance where applicable.
Record future due items only after verifying the schedule.
documents.urgency: Safety-related warnings or obvious defects require immediate inspection independent of routine intervals.
needed_information: Exact make/model/year/engine, current odometer, last service dates and odometer, and operating conditions.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and maintenance schedule
sources.reference: No generic mileage or time interval should replace the manufacturer's schedule.

documents.title: Pre-rental and post-rental vehicle inspection
documents.overview: A fleet release inspection is a documented condition check, not a substitute for scheduled service or mechanical diagnosis.
possible_causes: Missed damage, warning lights, tire concerns, incomplete records, or unresolved reported symptoms can be overlooked without a consistent checklist.
symptoms: New damage, warning indicators, abnormal noises, fluid leaks, tire concerns, or customer-reported symptoms.
checks: Record exterior/interior condition, warning lights, tires, visible leaks, mileage, fuel/charge level, and required equipment.
Review open maintenance work and service due status against verified records.
Do not release a vehicle with unresolved safety-critical concerns.
documents.urgency: Brake, steering, tire, severe overheating, oil-pressure, fuel-leak, or other safety-critical concerns require removing the vehicle from service until qualified inspection.
needed_information: Vehicle ID, dated inspection, odometer, checklist results, open work orders, and service schedule.

sources.name: Fleet inspection policy and vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: The operator should define a documented checklist and follow the manufacturer's requirements.

documents.title: Vehicle health assessment and missing diagnostic information
keywords: confirm car is safe based only on mileage
which parts of this rental vehicle should be inspected first
what parts should I inspect first
model score prove vehicle has no faults
reported symptoms versus technician confirmed faults
confirm vehicle passed inspection when no inspection record was supplied
documents.overview: A reliable health assessment combines verified vehicle identity, mileage, service history, inspection findings, and relevant diagnostic measurements. A short chat description or model score cannot establish overall vehicle condition.
possible_causes: Incomplete history, missing measurements, unverified user reports, or a model trained on different data can limit an assessment.
symptoms: A symptom should be recorded with when it occurs, warning indicators, and any inspection or scan results.
checks: Separate recorded facts, user-reported symptoms, model recommendations, and technician-confirmed faults.
Prioritize safety-critical symptoms for inspection.
Request make/model/year/engine, mileage, warning codes, service history, and symptom conditions.
documents.urgency: A low model score cannot establish that a vehicle is safe. Safety-critical symptoms must be addressed independently of model output.
needed_information: Vehicle identity, current mileage, service records, warning codes, inspection results, and symptom details.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information and verified fleet records
sources.reference: A model can use only the inputs and targets it was trained and validated to support.

documents.title: Interpreting maintenance model recommendations and scores
keywords: low model score prove vehicle is safe
documents.overview: A model recommendation is a statistical signal based on its training labels and supplied features. It is not a confirmed defect, calibrated failure probability, remaining useful life, or prediction of a failure date.
possible_causes: Scores may reflect patterns in training data and are limited by training coverage, feature quality, label quality, and the configured decision threshold.
symptoms: A flagged category means the model crossed its configured recommendation threshold; a low score does not prove that the vehicle is fault-free.
checks: Review the supplied feature values, threshold, service history, and a physical inspection.
Explain the model's actual recorded output; never infer a failed part or invent a probability.
documents.urgency: Use safety-critical symptoms and qualified inspection to determine immediate action; do not use model output alone to declare a vehicle safe.
needed_information: The model response, supplied features, model version, threshold, and relevant inspection/history data.

sources.name: Local maintenance model artifact and evaluation report
sources.reference: Use only outputs that the installed artifact actually returns; confirm limitations against its evaluation.

documents.title: Fleet maintenance prioritization and recurring issues
documents.overview: Fleet comparisons require authorized, comparable vehicle records and service history. A model can rank only the eligible records actually supplied to it.
possible_causes: Missing mileage, stale inspections, inconsistent labels, and incomplete maintenance history can distort prioritization or hide recurring issues.
symptoms: Repeated work orders, safety-critical findings, overdue verified service, and model recommendations are distinct evidence types and should be reported separately.
checks: Compare dated records with vehicle-specific schedules.
Prioritize confirmed safety defects and urgent symptoms before routine predictive recommendations.
Report analyzed, rejected, and missing records rather than treating missing data as low risk.
documents.urgency: Do not infer that an unreported vehicle has no maintenance need; flag missing or stale records for follow-up.
needed_information: Authorized fleet records, vehicle identities, mileage, service dates, inspection findings, and supported model inputs.

sources.name: Authorized fleet maintenance records and vehicle-specific schedules
sources.reference: Fleet conclusions are limited to the records supplied by the authorized backend.

documents.title: Difference between a symptom, diagnostic code, and confirmed fault
keywords: difference between symptom DTC and diagnosis
confirm cause before replacing a part
documents.overview: A symptom is an observed behavior, a diagnostic code is a recorded indication, and a confirmed fault requires appropriate testing or inspection. They should not be presented as interchangeable.
possible_causes: Different faults can create similar symptoms, and one code can have several possible causes.
symptoms: Noise, warning light, vibration, odor, or changed performance are observations to document, not proof of a specific failed component.
checks: Record the condition and exact warning/code.
Use manufacturer diagnostic procedures and confirm findings before repair.
Seek a qualified technician when safety or specialized testing is involved.
documents.urgency: Treat warning lights and safety-critical symptoms according to the owner's manual; severe brake, steering, overheating, oil-pressure, or fuel symptoms require prompt action.
needed_information: Exact vehicle, observed symptom, warning codes, conditions, and test or inspection results.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information
sources.reference: Diagnosis requires the correct procedure and supporting test results.

documents.title: Hybrid and electric vehicle high-voltage safety
keywords: do hybrids and electric cars use only one coolant circuit
documents.overview: Hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and battery-electric vehicles can contain high-voltage traction circuits in addition to ordinary low-voltage electrical systems. Their layouts, isolation methods, interlocks, stored energy, and technician requirements are vehicle-specific; a symptom or warning does not make exposed components safe to touch.
component_functions: A traction battery stores energy for an electric drive system; a battery-management system monitors and controls it.
An inverter and electric motor convert and use electrical energy; hybrid designs may also include an engine and separate power paths.
Some vehicles have multiple thermal circuits for the traction battery, power electronics, motor, engine, or cabin; one reservoir must not be assumed to serve all circuits.
possible_causes: A warning may relate to low-voltage supply, charging equipment, thermal management, isolation monitoring, battery-management controls, wiring, or a high-voltage component; the displayed message and vehicle-specific diagnostic data are needed.
symptoms: A high-voltage or hybrid-system warning, reduced propulsion, charging interruption, unusual heat, smoke, odor, crash damage, or fluid intrusion warrants cautious handling.
checks: Do not open a traction-battery enclosure, touch orange cables/connectors, probe high-voltage terminals, defeat an interlock, or attempt isolation yourself.
For smoke, fire, unusual heat, crash damage, or hissing/odor, move people away, stop using or charging the vehicle if safe, and contact emergency responders or qualified assistance.
Use only the owner's manual for user-level instructions such as warning response, towing, and charging; do not assume conventional jump-start or fluid-check procedures apply.
diagnostic_steps: A trained high-voltage technician must identify the exact vehicle architecture and follow its manufacturer's isolation, verification, PPE, and service procedures before working on high-voltage components.
Do not infer battery failure from a warning code alone; diagnosis may involve scan data and manufacturer-defined isolation, electrical, thermal, and control-system tests.
professional_diagnostics: High-voltage diagnosis and battery opening require appropriately trained and equipped personnel using exact manufacturer service information; this knowledge base does not provide an isolation procedure.
vehicle_variations: Battery-electric, hybrid, and plug-in hybrid architectures differ; even vehicles of the same make may have different battery, inverter, charging, and thermal layouts by year and trim.
known_unknowns: No make, model, year, warning message, or service document was supplied, so no component-level diagnosis or procedure can be given.
documents.urgency: Do not touch or service exposed high-voltage components. For smoke, fire, unusual heat, collision damage, or electrical hazard, move away and seek emergency or qualified assistance. Do not charge a damaged or abnormally hot vehicle.
needed_information: Make/model/year and powertrain type, exact dashboard message, whether charging or propulsion is affected, and any collision, flooding, smoke, heat, or odor.
documents.source_gap: No exact manufacturer owner or high-voltage service document was supplied or retrieved; only general hazard boundaries are provided.

documents.title: Cabin heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning concerns
keywords: hybrid heater and defroster stopped working
documents.overview: Cabin heating and air-conditioning depend on airflow, heat exchangers, doors and controls, and—in vehicles with conventional A/C—a sealed refrigerant circuit. A warm vent or weak airflow does not by itself identify a failed compressor or refrigerant leak.
component_functions: The blower moves air through cabin filters and heat exchangers.
A heater may use engine coolant, an electric heater, or another vehicle-specific heat source; blend doors route air through the selected path.
Air conditioning transfers cabin heat through a refrigerant circuit with components such as a compressor, condenser, metering device, and evaporator, but architectures vary.
possible_causes: Weak airflow can result from a blower, control, filter, door, or electrical issue.
Warm air with normal airflow can involve control settings, blend-door operation, heat-source availability, refrigerant-circuit performance, or a sensor/control fault.
Odor, water, noise, or intermittent behavior may have several causes and requires inspection.
symptoms: Compare airflow strength at available fan settings, vent temperature, selected mode, outside conditions, and whether the concern affects heating, cooling, or both.
checks: Confirm the selected temperature, fan, recirculation, and outlet settings; consult the vehicle manual for normal operation.
Do not handle refrigerant, loosen A/C fittings, bypass pressure switches, or probe moving/electrically controlled components.
If cabin heat is lost at the same time as engine overheating, treat the engine-temperature warning as urgent and follow the cooling-system safety guidance.
diagnostic_steps: A qualified technician may inspect filters, airflow doors, blower controls, electrical supplies, temperature sensors, and system performance using vehicle-specific procedures.
Refrigerant identification, pressure testing, recovery, leak repair, and charging require suitable equipment and applicable legal/technical procedures; a pressure reading alone is not a diagnosis.
professional_diagnostics: A/C refrigerant service and suspected refrigerant leaks should be handled by appropriately equipped personnel; exact refrigerant and charge specification are vehicle-specific.
vehicle_variations: HVAC controls, refrigerants, heat sources, auxiliary heaters, and multi-zone layouts vary by model; hybrid and electric vehicles may use heat pumps or high-voltage compressors.
known_unknowns: No vehicle identity, refrigerant label, test readings, or manufacturer procedure was supplied; no fluid type, charge amount, pressure, or repair procedure is asserted.
documents.urgency: A cabin comfort fault alone is often not an immediate mechanical emergency, but impaired windshield defrosting, burning odor, smoke, electrical overheating, or concurrent engine overheating requires stopping safely and arranging inspection.
needed_information: Make/model/year, powertrain, heating or cooling complaint, airflow strength, selected mode, warning messages, odors/noises, recent service, and ambient conditions.
documents.source_gap: No exact manufacturer HVAC information or refrigerant service data was available; guidance is limited to general system roles and safe boundaries.

documents.title: Exhaust leaks, emissions controls, and diesel particulate filters
documents.overview: The exhaust system carries combustion gases away and may include oxygen sensors, a catalytic converter, exhaust-gas recirculation, and diesel aftertreatment such as a particulate filter. A warning or code identifies a condition to investigate, not a component proven failed.
component_functions: An oxygen sensor reports exhaust-related measurements to the control system; the code or reading does not alone prove sensor failure.
A catalytic converter and, where fitted, a diesel particulate filter treat or capture specified exhaust constituents.
Diesel filter regeneration and EGR operation are managed according to the particular engine and aftertreatment design.
possible_causes: A leak, damaged wiring, sensor circuit, air/fuel issue, engine misfire, exhaust restriction, or aftertreatment operating condition may cause an emissions warning or changed exhaust behavior.
A DPF warning may reflect loading or a system fault; the exact message and manufacturer procedure determine safe next steps.
symptoms: Exhaust odor, ticking or hissing, smoke, reduced power, warning messages, or a scan code can help guide inspection but do not confirm a failed catalyst, sensor, EGR valve, or filter.
checks: If exhaust fumes enter the cabin, stop using the vehicle and get fresh air; carbon monoxide cannot be reliably detected by smell.
Record the exact warning and diagnostic codes, including pending status and freeze-frame data, before clearing anything.
Do not block, remove, bypass, or modify emissions equipment, and do not initiate an unfamiliar regeneration procedure.
diagnostic_steps: A technician may inspect for leaks, review engine and aftertreatment data, verify sensor circuits and plausibility, and follow the exact manufacturer diagnostic tree before parts replacement.
After repair, confirm the fault is corrected and the applicable readiness/monitoring checks complete using the vehicle-specific method.
professional_diagnostics: Exhaust leaks, catalyst/DPF faults, sensor diagnosis, and regeneration procedures require exact vehicle service information and suitable diagnostic equipment.
vehicle_variations: Aftertreatment hardware and regeneration behavior differ by gasoline/diesel engine, model year, market, and duty cycle; motorcycles may use different or simpler exhaust-control systems.
known_unknowns: No exact vehicle, code, exhaust measurement, or warning message was supplied, so no specific component or regeneration procedure can be identified.
documents.urgency: Exhaust fumes in the cabin, smoke, fire risk, severe power loss, or a flashing engine warning requires stopping safely and prompt assistance. Do not run an engine in an enclosed space.
needed_information: Make/model/year, engine and fuel type, exact warning/code, symptoms and operating conditions, recent repairs, and scan/freeze-frame results.
documents.source_gap: No vehicle-specific emissions or aftertreatment service procedure was available; no code-specific definition or regeneration steps are asserted.

documents.title: Motorcycle chain, belt, and shaft final-drive concerns
documents.overview: Many motorcycles use a chain and sprockets, a belt, or a shaft final drive. Wear, lubrication, alignment, tension, and inspection requirements depend on the exact drive design and manufacturer procedure.
component_functions: A chain and sprockets transmit engine torque to the rear wheel and require model-specific inspection and maintenance.
Belt and shaft drives have different inspection and service needs; chain adjustment guidance must not be applied to them.
possible_causes: Noise, tight spots, excess slack, uneven wear, damaged links or teeth, misalignment, lubrication condition, or wheel/drive faults can affect final-drive operation.
symptoms: Clicking, tight spots during wheel rotation, snatch or lash, visible damage, unusual slack, or a change after wheel service warrants inspection.
checks: Do not touch or adjust a moving chain. Keep hands, clothing, and tools away from the drive while the engine is running.
With the motorcycle secured and engine off, perform only the inspection described by its owner's manual; do not assume one slack value applies to all bikes.
Do not ride with a damaged, binding, or visibly unsafe final drive; arrange qualified inspection.
diagnostic_steps: A technician should verify chain/belt/shaft type, wheel alignment, tension or play at the specified measurement point, wear limits, and fastener procedures using the exact model service information.
professional_diagnostics: Adjustment values, lubrication products, wear limits, and axle torque are model-specific and are not provided here.
vehicle_variations: Motorcycle chain, belt, and shaft-drive layouts differ from passenger-car drivetrains; rider load and suspension position may affect specified chain measurement procedure.
known_unknowns: No motorcycle make, model, year, drive type, measured condition, or manual was supplied; no adjustment specification is asserted.
documents.urgency: A damaged or binding motorcycle final drive can cause loss of propulsion or control. Do not ride if the drive appears damaged or unsafe.
needed_information: Motorcycle make/model/year, chain/belt/shaft type, noise or visible damage, inspection findings, recent wheel work, and the manual's specified check.
documents.source_gap: No exact motorcycle owner's or service manual was supplied or retrieved; adjustment values and repair instructions remain unavailable.
